'''Joseph Yanai''' ({{Langx|he|יוסף ינאי}}) is a researcher pioneering in studying the reversal of neurobehavioral [[birth defect]]s in animal models.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Vigoda |first2=Myles J. |last3=Ornoy |first3=Asher |date=August 2019 |title=Reversal of neurobehavioral teratogenicity in animal models and human: Three decades of progress |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |volume=150 |pages=328–342 |doi=10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |pmid=31207281 |s2cid=189820103 |issn=0361-9230|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He serves as a professor and Director of the Ross Laboratory for Studies in Neural Birth Defects at the Department of Medical Neurobiology, The [[Institute For Medical Research, Israel-Canada]] (IMRIC) at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School Jerusalem, Israel and was also appointed as adjunct professor, Department of [[Pharmacology]] and Cancer Biology, [[Duke University School of Medicine]], Durham, NC, US.

== Education ==
Yanai was born in [[Rehovot]], Israel in 1944. After graduating from the [[Mikveh Israel]] Agricultural High School, he received his BSc Agr. in agriculture and genetics at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] in 1967 and both his MA in 1970 and [[PhD]] in 1971 from the [[University of Colorado Boulder]].

== Professional career ==
* Professor, Department of Medical Neurobiology, [[Hebrew University]], [[Hadassah Medical School]], Jerusalem, since 1978.
* [[Adjunct professor]], Department of Pharmacology and Cancer Biology, [[Duke University School of Medicine]], [[Durham, North Carolina]], 1991-2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://medicine.ekmd.huji.ac.il/en/research/josephy/Pages/default.aspx|title=Professor Joseph Yanai|website=The Hebrew University of Jerusalem}}</ref>
* Director, Ross Laboratory for Studies in Neural Birth Defects, Department of Neurobiology, Hebrew University Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem, since 1987.

== Research work ==
Since 1973, he has been among the forerunners in the study of behavioral birth defects.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=December 1973 |title=Behavior genetics association abstracts |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01070223 |journal=Behavior Genetics |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=393–419 |doi=10.1007/bf01070223 |s2cid=189854750 |issn=0001-8244|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His novel approach was to study the mechanism by which certain neuroteratogens induce their deleterious effect, focusing on behavioral defects that are mechanistically related to septohippocampal cholinergic innervation.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=December 1973 |title=Behavior genetics association abstracts |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01070223 |journal=Behavior Genetics |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=393–419 |doi=10.1007/bf01070223 |s2cid=189854750 |issn=0001-8244|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The results showed alterations in cholinergic neurotransmission cascade converging into the abolishment of the cholinergic receptor-induced activation/translocation PKC activity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Beer |first2=Avital |last3=Huleihel |first3=Rabab |last4=Izrael |first4=Michal |last5=Katz |first5=Sofia |last6=Levi |first6=Yaarit |last7=Rozenboim |first7=Israel |last8=Yaniv |first8=Shiri P. |last9=Slotkin |first9=Theodore A. |date=October 2004 |title=Convergent Effects on Cell Signaling Mechanisms Mediate the Actions of Different Neurobehavioral Teratogens: Alterations in Cholinergic Regulation of Protein Kinase C in Chick and Avian Models |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1196/annals.1316.074 |journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences |volume=1025 |issue=1 |pages=595–601 |doi=10.1196/annals.1316.074 |pmid=15542768 |bibcode=2004NYASA1025..595Y |s2cid=10927050 |issn=0077-8923|url-access=subscription }}</ref> By ascertaining the mechanisms of the neuroteratogenicity, he pointed in his book “neurobehavioral teratology.”
<ref>{{Cite book |title=Neurobehavioral teratology |date=1984 |publisher=Elsevier |editor=Joseph Yanai |isbn=0-444-80516-8 |location=Amsterdam |oclc=10275574}}</ref> to the future of the field by establishing the concept of "Neurobehavioral teratology. Furthermore, Yanai argued that understanding the mechanism of the developmental defect will eventually enable its reversal, a concept that seemed like science fiction in 1984.

Specifically since 1987, Yanai has developed animal models for the reversal of neurobehavioral birth defects, starting with manipulation of A10 septal dopaminergic innervation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Laxer |first2=Uri |last3=Pick |first3=Chaim G. |last4=Trombka |first4=David |date=August 1989 |title=Dopaminergic denervation reverses behavioral deficits induced by prenatal exposure to phenobarbital |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0165-3806(89)90080-1 |journal=Developmental Brain Research |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=255–261 |doi=10.1016/0165-3806(89)90080-1 |pmid=2505945 |issn=0165-3806|url-access=subscription }}</ref> nicotine therapy,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beer |first1=Avital |last2=Slotkin |first2=Theodore A |last3=Seidler |first3=Frederic J |last4=Aldridge |first4=Justin E |last5=Yanai |first5=Joseph |date=2004-10-20 |title=Nicotine Therapy in Adulthood Reverses the Synaptic and Behavioral Deficits Elicited by Prenatal Exposure to Phenobarbital |journal=Neuropsychopharmacology |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=156–165 |doi=10.1038/sj.npp.1300582 |pmid=15496940 |issn=0893-133X|doi-access=free }}</ref> but most significantly, by transplantation of cells to the impaired brain. These included fetal differentiated brain cells (neural grafting),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Pick |first2=Chaim G. |date=1988 |title=Neuron transplantation reverses phenobarbital-induced behavioral birth defects in mice |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0736-5748(88)90046-9 |journal=International Journal of Developmental Neuroscience |volume=6 |issue=5 |pages=409–416 |doi=10.1016/0736-5748(88)90046-9 |pmid=3202000 |s2cid=23370083 |issn=0736-5748|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and in subsequent studies, stem cells of various origins: embryonic, neural stem cells,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kazma |first1=Meital |last2=Izrael |first2=Michal |last3=Revel |first3=Michel |last4=Chebath |first4=Judith |last5=Yanai |first5=Joseph |date=2010-02-01 |title=Survival, differentiation, and reversal of heroin neurobehavioral teratogenicity in mice by transplanted neural stem cells derived from embryonic stem cells |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/jnr.22193 |journal=Journal of Neuroscience Research |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=315–323 |doi=10.1002/jnr.22193 |pmid=19746435 |s2cid=24682086 |issn=0360-4012|url-access=subscription }}</ref> subventricular stem cells,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turgeman |first1=Gadi |last2=Pinkas |first2=Adi |last3=Slotkin |first3=Theodore A. |last4=Tfilin |first4=Matanel |last5=Langford |first5=Rachel |last6=Yanai |first6=Joseph |date=2011-04-21 |title=Reversal of chlorpyrifos neurobehavioral teratogenicity in mice by allographic transplantation of adult subventricular zone-derived neural stem cells |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/jnr.22631 |journal=Journal of Neuroscience Research |volume=89 |issue=8 |pages=1185–1193 |doi=10.1002/jnr.22631 |pmid=21520219 |s2cid=3424029 |issn=0360-4012|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and mesenchymal stem cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Vigoda |first2=Myles J. |last3=Ornoy |first3=Asher |date=August 2019 |title=Reversal of neurobehavioral teratogenicity in animal models and human: Three decades of progress |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |volume=150 |pages=328–342 |doi=10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |pmid=31207281 |s2cid=189820103 |issn=0361-9230|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Stem cell therapy may reverse brain birth defects |url=https://www.oneindia.com/2008/12/30/stem-cell-therapy-may-reverse-brain-birth-defects.html |website=Oneindia.com |language=en |date=30 December 2008}}</ref>
Transplantation of cells of all types reversed the prenatally-induced behavioral deficits and the mechanistically related neural alterations. Further studies suggested that one major mechanism by which the stem cells exert their therapeutic action is by enhancing neurogenesis. More recently, Yanai expanded his research on early development to include parental preconception exposure.<ref>{{cite web |title=Health Scan: Stem cell therapy may reverse brain defects |url=https://www.jpost.com/health-and-sci-tech/health/health-scan-stem-cell-therapy-may-reverse-brain-defects |website=The Jerusalem Post |date=11 January 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ben-Shaanan |first1=T L |last2=Ben-Hur |first2=T |last3=Yanai |first3=J |date=2007-09-18 |title=Transplantation of neural progenitors enhances production of endogenous cells in the impaired brain |journal=Molecular Psychiatry |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=222–231 |doi=10.1038/sj.mp.4002084 |pmid=17876325 |s2cid=12784221 |issn=1359-4184|doi-access=free }}</ref>

These findings were published in the leading journal (for example ''[[Molecular Psychiatry]]'',<ref>Ben-Shaanan, TL, Ben-Hur, T, and Yanai, J.: “Transplantation of neural progenitors enhances production of endogeneous cells in the impaired brain”. Molecular Psychiatry, September 18, 2007. Vol. 13, No. 2, pp222-231</ref>) and received a widespread media attention (external links<ref>{{cite web |title=Hebrew University Scientists Succeed Through Stem Cell Therapy in Reversing Brain Birth Defects |url=https://www.technologynetworks.com/cell-science/news/hebrew-university-scientists-succeed-through-stem-cell-therapy-in-reversing-brain-birth-defects-196809 |website=Technology Networks |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Stem Cells Undo Birth Defects |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2009/01/07/216614/stem-cells-undo-birth-defects/ |website=MIT Technology Review |language=en}}</ref>) and presented in an invited major address, at the  international conferences in [[San Antonio, Texas]], in June 2016.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yanai |first=Joseph |date=May 2016 |title=Fortieth Anniversary Annual Meeting of the Developmental Neurotoxicology Society Held in Conjunction with the 56th Annual Meeting of the Teratology Society Grand Hyatt San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas June 25–29, 2016 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.ntt.2016.04.003 |journal=Neurotoxicology and Teratology |volume=55 |pages=58–75 |doi=10.1016/j.ntt.2016.04.003 |issn=0892-0362|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Review of Yanai’s work and the progress in reversal of neurobehavioral teratology that was advanced by other laboratories was published in 2019<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yanai |first1=Joseph |last2=Vigoda |first2=Myles J. |last3=Ornoy |first3=Asher |date=August 2019 |title=Reversal of neurobehavioral teratogenicity in animal models and human: Three decades of progress |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |volume=150 |pages=328–342 |doi=10.1016/j.brainresbull.2019.06.009 |pmid=31207281 |s2cid=189820103 |issn=0361-9230|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and in Basel, Switzerland, in February 2017.
